claim: Homeostatic regulation is essential for stable neuronal function.
source: Homeostatic regulation is essential for stable neuronal function.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field of neuroscience.

claim: Several synaptic mechanisms of homeostatic plasticity have been described.
source: Several synaptic mechanisms of homeostatic plasticity have been described, but the functional properties of synapses involved in homeostasis are unknown.
evidence: This refers to existing literature on homeostatic plasticity mechanisms.

claim: The functional properties of synapses involved in homeostasis are unknown.
source: Several synaptic mechanisms of homeostatic plasticity have been described, but the functional properties of synapses involved in homeostasis are unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Longitudinal two-photon functional imaging of dendritic spine calcium signals was used in visual and retrosplenial cortices of awake adult mice.
source: We used longitudinal two-photon functional imaging of dendritic spine calcium signals in visual and retrosplenial cortices of awake adult mice to quantify the sensory deprivation-induced changes in the responses of functionally identified spines.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Spines whose activity selectively correlated with intrinsic network activity underwent tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α)-dependent homeostatic increases in their response amplitudes.
source: We found that spines whose activity selectively correlated with intrinsic network activity underwent tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α)-dependent homeostatic increases in their response amplitudes, but spines identified as responsive to sensory stimulation did not.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spines identified as responsive to sensory stimulation did not undergo homeostatic increases in their response amplitudes.
source: We found that spines whose activity selectively correlated with intrinsic network activity underwent tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α)-dependent homeostatic increases in their response amplitudes, but spines identified as responsive to sensory stimulation did not.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: An increase in global sensory-evoked responses was observed following sensory deprivation.
source: We observed an increase in the global sensory-evoked responses following sensory deprivation, despite the fact that the identified sensory inputs did not strengthen.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Global sensory-evoked responses correlated with the strength of network-correlated inputs.
source: Instead, global sensory-evoked responses correlated with the strength of network-correlated inputs.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing correlation between two measured variables.

claim: Homeostatic regulation of global responses is mediated through changes to intrinsic network-correlated inputs rather than changes to identified sensory inputs.
source: Our results suggest that homeostatic regulation of global responses is mediated through changes to intrinsic network-correlated inputs rather than changes to identified sensory inputs thought to drive sensory processing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Homeostatic regulation of neuronal firing levels is a critical feature of neural circuits.
source: Homeostatic regulation of neuronal firing levels is a critical feature of neural circuits.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus.

claim: Homeostatic regulation allows for prolonged stable function during changing activity levels associated with ongoing Hebbian plasticity, changes in sensory drive or input loss.
source: It allows for prolonged stable function during changing activity levels associated with ongoing Hebbian plasticity, changes in sensory drive or input loss (Keck et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Impairment of homeostatic regulation is thought to result in prolonged periods of excessive neuronal hyper- or hypoactivity.
source: The impairment of homeostatic regulation is thought to result in prolonged periods of excessive neuronal hyper- or hypoactivity, which may impair network function (Frere and Slutsky, 2018; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2014; Marder and Prinz, 2002; Tetzlaff et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2020; Zenke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Homeostatic regulation occurs through plastic changes to a broad range of synaptic, intrinsic, cellular, and network-level properties.
source: Homeostatic regulation occurs through plastic changes to a broad range of synaptic, intrinsic, cellular, and network-level properties (Barnes et al., 2015; Bridi et al., 2020; Bridi et al., 2018; Gainey and Feldman, 2017; Joseph and Turrigiano, 2017; Keck et al., 2017; Lee and Kirkwood, 2019; Ma et al., 2019; Turrigiano, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Homeostatic changes must facilitate rebalancing of activity while maintaining the underlying circuits established for ongoing sensory processing.
source: These changes must facilitate rebalancing of activity while maintaining the underlying circuits established for ongoing sensory processing (Chen et al., 2013a; Iacaruso et al., 2017), as well as for learned (Jurjut et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2020; Poort et al., 2015) and innate behaviors (Branco and Redgrave, 2020; Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Previous work in adult animals has shown that synaptic homeostatic changes occur in only a subset of synapses.
source: Previous work in adult animals has shown that synaptic homeostatic changes occur in only a subset of synapses (Barnes et al., 2017) or via additive changes (Goel and Lee, 2007), as opposed to multiplicative changes across the entire population described for some homeostatic mechanisms during development and the critical period (Desai et al., 2002; Kaneko et al., 2008; Turrigiano, 2017; Turrigiano et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Sensory cortices in adult mice are multimodal and receive multiple sensory inputs.
source: Sensory cortices in adult mice are known to be multimodal and receive multiple sensory inputs (Ibrahim et al., 2016; Iurilli et al., 2012; Knöpfel et al., 2019; Todd et al., 2016; Vann et al., 2009; Yoshitake et al., 2013), as well as intrinsic contextual and intracortical inputs (Fiser et al., 2016; Khan and Hofer, 2018; Miller et al., 2014; Okun et al., 2015; Pakan et al., 2016; Pakan et al., 2018b; Petrus et al., 2015; Roth et al., 2016; Saleem et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Large populations of neurons in visual cortex have a strong correlation or coupling with the average network activity.
source: Large populations of neurons in visual cortex have a strong correlation or coupling with the average network activity, which is thought to be largely non-sensory and represent contextual input that may be associated with behavioral state (Okun et al., 2015; Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: High levels of network coupling are correlated with a higher probability of local intracortical connections between neurons.
source: High levels of network coupling are correlated with a higher probability of local intracortical connections between neurons (Okun et al., 2015) and could also reflect the presence of other common non-sensory inputs (Yoshimura et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Chronic two-photon imaging in awake adult mice expressing GCaMP6s was used to examine the functional properties of dendritic spines.
source: We used chronic two-photon imaging in awake adult mice expressing the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6s (see Methods) to examine the functional properties of dendritic spines that undergo functional plasticity following sensory deprivation.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Functional calcium signals in dendritic spines were repeatedly measured on the distal tufts (in layer 2/3) of layer 5 pyramidal cells in primary monocular visual cortex before and after sensory deprivation via enucleation of the contralateral eye.
source: Over a span of 4 days, we repeatedly measured functional calcium signals in dendritic spines on the distal tufts (in layer 2/3) of layer 5 pyramidal cells in primary monocular visual cortex before and after sensory deprivation via enucleation of the contralateral eye (Figure 1A–C; Barnes et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and references Figure 1.

claim: Approximately 20% of spines in the contralateral visual cortex became inactive 12 hr after monocular deprivation.
source: Consistent with previous work (Barnes et al., 2017), we found that approximately 20% of spines in the contralateral visual cortex became inactive 12 hr after monocular deprivation, with the number of inactive spines decreasing over time (Figure 1D, see Methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, consistent with previous work.

claim: The number of inactive spines decreased over time following monocular deprivation.
source: Consistent with previous work (Barnes et al., 2017), we found that approximately 20% of spines in the contralateral visual cortex became inactive 12 hr after monocular deprivation, with the number of inactive spines decreasing over time (Figure 1D, see Methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Persistent spines increased their functional response amplitudes on average.
source: On average, the persistent (active at all time points) spines increased their functional response amplitudes (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The increased amplitude of spine responses was blocked by an intraperitoneal injection of a dominant negative form of TNF-α.
source: The increased amplitude of spine responses was blocked by an intraperitoneal injection of a dominant negative form of TNF-α (Figure 1A and F), suggesting this effect is dependent on TNF-α.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing the effect of TNF-α inhibition.

claim: The spine response amplitude increase following deprivation is dependent on TNF-α.
source: The increased amplitude of spine responses was blocked by an intraperitoneal injection of a dominant negative form of TNF-α (Figure 1A and F), suggesting this effect is dependent on TNF-α.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental result that TNF-α inhibition blocks the amplitude increase.

claim: Following deprivation, there were no changes over time in the average frequency of responses at the population level.
source: Following deprivation, we found no changes over time in the average frequency of responses at the population level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: There was no correlation between changes in frequency and amplitude within individual spines.
source: We observed no correlation between changes in frequency and amplitude within individual spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the changes in frequency are not likely to be driving the changes in amplitude within a single spine.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Changes in frequency are not likely to be driving the changes in amplitude within a single spine.
source: We observed no correlation between changes in frequency and amplitude within individual spines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the changes in frequency are not likely to be driving the changes in amplitude within a single spine.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between frequency and amplitude changes.

claim: Not all spines undergo a TNF-α-dependent strengthening following deprivation.
source: We have previously used structural imaging of spine size as an in vivo proxy for synaptic strength and shown that not all spines undergo a TNF-α-dependent strengthening following deprivation (Barnes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Spines with the lowest visual responsiveness prior to deprivation underwent the strongest functional strengthening after deprivation.
source: When we examined the functional strengthening of all of the spines, we found an inverse relationship, such that the spines with the lowest visual responsiveness prior to deprivation underwent the strongest functional strengthening after deprivation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Only a subset of spines increased their functional responses following deprivation.
source: Consistent with our previous work (Barnes et al., 2017), we observed that only a subset of spines increased their functional responses (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, consistent with previous work.

claim: A majority of spines that were responsive to the sparse noise stimulus also responded to drifting gratings (97%).
source: We found that a majority of spines that were responsive to the sparse noise stimulus also responded to drifting gratings (97%).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Most spines (89%) had a significant correlation with the network signal.
source: In our population of spines, we found that most spines (89%) had a significant correlation with the network signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: All visually responsive spines had a significant correlation with the network signal.
source: This included the visually responsive spines, all of which had a significant correlation with the network signal (see Methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: 24% of spines were classified as visually responsive.
source: All spines with time-locked responses to visual stimuli at above chance levels (see Methods) were classified as visually responsive spines (24%; Figure 2B), even though their activity also correlated with the network signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: 65% of spines were classified as network-correlated.
source: Spines with activity that correlated with the network signal, but did not have visually-evoked responses, were classified as network-correlated (65%).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: 11% of spines were classified as unclassified.
source: The remainder of spines neither responded to the visual stimuli nor correlated with the network activity, which we refer to as unclassified (11%; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Unclassified spines showed no evidence of significant correlations with pupil movement, pupil dilation, or whisker movement above chance.
source: We tested whether these unclassified spines were correlated with other behavioral measures, such as pupil movement, pupil dilation (diameter), and whisker movement, and found no evidence of significant correlations above chance (see Methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There were no significant differences in the average activity in the three groups of spines (network-correlated, visually responsive, unclassified) prior to deprivation.
source: There were no significant differences in the average activity in the three groups of spines prior to deprivation (measured as the area under the curve of the ΔF/F0 fluorescence signal; comparison between network-correlated, visually responsive and unclassified spine activity, one-way ANOVA, p=0.232).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: All of the branches measured had all three types of spines (visually responsive, network-correlated, unclassified).
source: All of the branches that we measured had all three types of spines (visually responsive, network-correlated, unclassified).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The local spatial organization of functional response properties of dendritic spines were not different from chance within individual dendritic branches.
source: Within individual dendritic branches, we found that the local spatial organization of functional response properties (visually responsive, network-correlated, unclassified) of the dendritic spines were not different from chance (Figure 2D–F, see Methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no evidence of an increase in the amplitude of the persistent spines identified as visually responsive following deprivation.
source: Consistent with our earlier finding (Figure 2C), we found no evidence of an increase in the amplitude of the persistent spines identified as visually responsive (Figure 3A), or of the persistent unclassified spines (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no evidence of an increase in the amplitude of the persistent unclassified spines following deprivation.
source: Consistent with our earlier finding (Figure 2C), we found no evidence of an increase in the amplitude of the persistent spines identified as visually responsive (Figure 3A), or of the persistent unclassified spines (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Following deprivation there was an increase in the response amplitude of persistent network-correlated spines.
source: However, following deprivation there was an increase in the response amplitude of persistent network-correlated spines (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: A decrease in the frequency of responses of visually responsive spines was observed over time following deprivation.
source: While the average frequency of responses did not change following deprivation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), we examined if functional groups of spines had changes in response frequency and observed a decrease in the frequency of responses of visually responsive spines over time following deprivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: A decrease in the integral of activity for visually responsive spines was observed over time following deprivation.
source: When we examined the integral of the activity trace (which combines amplitude and frequency) over time following deprivation, we observed a decrease for visually responsive spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), no change for unclassified spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), and an increase for network-correlated spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: No change in the integral of activity for unclassified spines was observed over time following deprivation.
source: When we examined the integral of the activity trace (which combines amplitude and frequency) over time following deprivation, we observed a decrease for visually responsive spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), no change for unclassified spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), and an increase for network-correlated spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: An increase in the integral of activity for network-correlated spines was observed over time following deprivation.
source: When we examined the integral of the activity trace (which combines amplitude and frequency) over time following deprivation, we observed a decrease for visually responsive spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), no change for unclassified spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), and an increase for network-correlated spines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: A strong increase in the fraction of inactive visually responsive spines was found after deprivation.
source: We also found a strong increase in the fraction of inactive visually responsive spines after deprivation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The increase in spine loss previously reported following enucleation may include both spines that were visually responsive and network-correlated prior to deprivation.
source: These results suggest that the increase in spine loss previously reported following enucleation (Barnes et al., 2017) may include both spines that were visually responsive and network-correlated prior to deprivation (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and previous work.

claim: A sizeable fraction of visually responsive spines remains active after visual deprivation.
source: A sizeable fraction of visually responsive spines remains active after visual deprivation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Following sensory deprivation, responses to visual stimuli were no longer observed in the visually responsive spines.
source: It is important to note that following sensory deprivation, we no longer observed responses to visual stimuli in the visually responsive spines, since the feedforward input had been permanently removed.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The responses of the previously categorized visually responsive spines consisted of network responses following deprivation.
source: The responses of the previously categorized visually responsive spines consisted of network responses following deprivation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was no correlation between amplitude and frequency within individual spines in any of the groups (visually responsive, unclassified, network-correlated).
source: There was no correlation between amplitude and frequency within individual spines in any of the groups (Figure 3G–I), again suggesting that frequency decrease does not regulate changes in amplitude within individual spines in this paradigm.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Frequency decrease does not regulate changes in amplitude within individual spines in this paradigm.
source: There was no correlation between amplitude and frequency within individual spines in any of the groups (Figure 3G–I), again suggesting that frequency decrease does not regulate changes in amplitude within individual spines in this paradigm.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between frequency and amplitude changes.

claim: Network-correlated inputs, and not the identified visually responsive inputs, are homeostatically strengthened following sensory input loss.
source: Overall, these results suggest the network-correlated inputs, and not the identified visually responsive inputs, are homeostatically strengthened following sensory input loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The retrosplenial cortex (RSC) receives measurable auditory responsive and visually responsive inputs.
source: To investigate this issue, we used a multimodal brain area – the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) – which receives measurable auditory responsive and visually responsive inputs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: 92% of spines in RSC had activity that was correlated with the network signal.
source: Using the same classification approach as before (Figure 2, see Methods), we found that the activity of 92% of the spines was correlated with the network signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: 18.7% of spines in RSC had time-locked responses to visual stimuli.
source: Within this group, a subset of spines had time-locked responses to visual (18.7%) or auditory (15.9%) stimuli (Figure 4A) and the rest correlated only with the network signal (57.4%, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: 15.9% of spines in RSC had time-locked responses to auditory stimuli.
source: Within this group, a subset of spines had time-locked responses to visual (18.7%) or auditory (15.9%) stimuli (Figure 4A) and the rest correlated only with the network signal (57.4%, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: 57.4% of spines in RSC correlated only with the network signal.
source: Within this group, a subset of spines had time-locked responses to visual (18.7%) or auditory (15.9%) stimuli (Figure 4A) and the rest correlated only with the network signal (57.4%, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: 8% of spines in RSC were unclassified (no correlation with the network signal and no sensory-evoked responses).
source: The remaining 8% of spines were unclassified (no correlation with the network signal and no sensory-evoked responses).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Following reversible visual deprivation via dark exposure for 48 hr, an increase in the average spine response amplitude across the population was observed in RSC.
source: Following reversible visual deprivation via dark exposure for 48 hr (Figure 4B), we observed an increase in the average spine response amplitude across the population.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The increase in average spine response amplitude in RSC following dark exposure was TNF-α-dependent.
source: This response was TNF-α-dependent (Figure 4C), similar to what we observed in visual cortex following enucleation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: In RSC, an increase in the response amplitude of the network-correlated spines was observed following visual deprivation, but not in the visually responsive or unclassified spines.
source: When we examined the changes in the responses of functionally identified spines, we observed an increase in the response amplitude of the network-correlated spines, but not in the visually responsive or unclassified spines (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), consistent with our results in visual cortex (Figure 2C, Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: After visual deprivation, the auditory responsive spines did not undergo functional strengthening but maintained their baseline amplitude.
source: We then examined the responses of the auditory responsive spines, which represent an identified non-deprived sensory input. After visual deprivation, the auditory responsive spines did not undergo functional strengthening but maintained their baseline amplitude following visual deprivation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Following auditory deprivation, a TNF-α-dependent population increase in spine responses was observed in RSC.
source: To ensure that the strengthening effects that we observed were not exclusive to visual deprivation, we performed a complementary, but separate, experiment where we deprived mice of auditory input through reversible ear plugging for 48 hr and again measured post-deprivation spine responses in the RSC (Figure 4F). We observed a TNF-α-dependent population increase in spine responses (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Following auditory deprivation, network-correlated spines increased their responses, but there was no change in the response strength of either visually responsive or auditory responsive spines.
source: Similar to visual deprivation, network-correlated spines increased their responses following auditory deprivation (Figure 4H–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F), but there was no change in the response strength of either (non-deprived) visually responsive (Figure 4H) or (deprived) auditory responsive spines (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Increases in spine response amplitude predominantly occur in the spines whose activity correlated with the network signal and not in the spines which are responsive to the non-deprived or deprived sensory stimulation.
source: Together, these data suggest that increases in spine response amplitude predominantly occur in the spines whose activity correlated with the network signal and not in the spines which are responsive to the non-deprived or deprived sensory stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Following visual deprivation, there is a homeostatic increase in the cellular visually-evoked responses relative to baseline.
source: Previous work has shown that following visual deprivation, there is a homeostatic increase in the cellular visually-evoked responses relative to baseline (Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: This homeostatic response is hypothesized to occur through a presumed strengthening of the spared visual inputs.
source: Critically, this homeostatic response is hypothesized to occur through a presumed strengthening of the spared visual inputs (Kaneko et al., 2008; Keck et al., 2017; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007; Pandey et al., 2022; Turrigiano, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Following visual deprivation via dark exposure, the global dendritic responses in RSC to both visual and auditory stimulation were increased when compared with baseline measurements.
source: We found that following visual deprivation via dark exposure, the global dendritic responses in RSC to both visual and auditory stimulation were increased when compared with baseline measurements (Figure 4J), consistent with past results (Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, consistent with previous work.

claim: Neither the visually responsive nor auditory responsive spines increased their responses to the same respective stimuli following visual deprivation.
source: This was despite the fact that neither the visually responsive nor auditory responsive spines increased their responses to the same respective stimuli (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Both the global visually-evoked responses and individual visually responsive spines maintained their visual tuning before and after deprivation at levels comparable to control.
source: Both the global visually-evoked responses and individual visually responsive spines maintained their visual tuning before and after deprivation at levels comparable to control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Increases in global dendritic responses after deprivation were uncorrelated with the changes in visually-evoked spine responses on those dendrites.
source: Increases in global dendritic responses after deprivation were uncorrelated with the changes in visually-evoked spine responses on those dendrites, making it unlikely that increases in global dendritic responses were driven by increases in the strength of visually-evoked spine responses (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: It is unlikely that increases in global dendritic responses were driven by increases in the strength of visually-evoked spine responses.
source: Increases in global dendritic responses after deprivation were uncorrelated with the changes in visually-evoked spine responses on those dendrites, making it unlikely that increases in global dendritic responses were driven by increases in the strength of visually-evoked spine responses (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between global dendritic responses and visually-evoked spine responses.

claim: There was no relationship within a dendrite between changes in global dendritic responses and auditory-evoked spine responses.
source: There was also no relationship within a dendrite between changes in global dendritic responses and auditory-evoked spine responses (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Increases in global dendritic responses were correlated with an increase in the network-correlated spine activity on the same dendrites.
source: Conversely, increases in global dendritic responses were correlated with an increase in the network-correlated spine activity on the same dendrites (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Increases in sensory-evoked global dendritic responses are unlikely to result from increases in the response strength of the identified sensory responsive inputs.
source: Our results suggest that increases in sensory-evoked global dendritic responses are unlikely to result from increases in the response strength of the identified sensory responsive inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: A TNF-α-dependent increase in the functional responses of dendritic spines in awake mice was observed following sensory deprivation.
source: Here, we report a TNF-α-dependent increase in the functional responses of dendritic spines in awake mice following sensory deprivation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the experimental data.

claim: Dendritic spines whose activity is correlated with the network signal are strengthened following sensory deprivation, but spines identified as sensory responsive are not.
source: Surprisingly, when we examine the functional properties of spines that undergo strengthening, we find dendritic spines whose activity is correlated with the network signal are strengthened, but spines identified as sensory responsive are not.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the experimental data.

claim: The strengthening of network-correlated spines occurs over a similar time course and magnitude in both visual cortex and RSC and in response to different deprivation paradigms.
source: This strengthening of network-correlated spines occurs over a similar time course and magnitude in both visual cortex and RSC and in response to different deprivation paradigms.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the experimental data.

claim: A homeostatic increase in global sensory-evoked responses was observed following sensory deprivation, despite the fact that there was no increase in responses of sensory responsive spines.
source: Despite the fact that we do not see an increase in responses of sensory responsive spines, we do observe a homeostatic increase in global sensory-evoked responses following sensory deprivation.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the experimental data.

claim: The global increase in sensory-evoked responses is correlated with an increase in the response strength of network-correlated spines on those branches, but not of identified sensory responsive spines.
source: This global increase is correlated with an increase in the response strength of network-correlated spines on those branches, but not of identified sensory responsive spines.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the experimental data.

claim: In vivo synaptic homeostasis during adulthood occurs in a functional subset of inputs, specifically those correlated only with network activity, rather than the identified sensory responsive inputs that are thought to drive sensory processing.
source: Our findings suggest that in vivo synaptic homeostasis during adulthood occurs in a functional subset of inputs, specifically those correlated only with network activity, rather than the identified sensory responsive inputs that are thought to drive sensory processing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The homeostatic increase in sensory-evoked responses observed after deprivation in adult mice is not associated with increases in the response strength of identified sensory responsive inputs.
source: Our results suggest that the homeostatic increase in sensory-evoked responses observed after deprivation in adult mice is not associated with increases in the response strength of identified sensory responsive inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: A correlation was observed between increases in global sensory-evoked activity levels and increases in the functional response strength of network-correlated spines.
source: Instead, we observe a correlation between increases in global sensory-evoked activity levels and increases in the functional response strength of network-correlated spines.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The strengthened network connections may serve to amplify intrinsic activity, keeping cells closer to the threshold for action potential generation and thereby making incoming sensory responsive inputs more likely to elicit the observed sensory-evoked increases in post-synaptic activity.
source: One possibility is that the strengthened network connections serve to amplify intrinsic activity, keeping cells closer to the threshold for action potential generation and thereby making incoming sensory responsive inputs more likely to elicit the observed sensory-evoked increases in post-synaptic activity.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed findings.

claim: Previous work has shown that homeostatic recovery at the level of small networks of cells is mediated by increases in the intrinsic network activity.
source: In line with this idea, previous work has shown that homeostatic recovery at the level of small networks of cells is mediated by increases in the intrinsic network activity (Barnes et al., 2015) and that intrinsic network activity is amplified within these interconnected neural ensembles (Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Intrinsic network activity is amplified within interconnected neural ensembles.
source: In line with this idea, previous work has shown that homeostatic recovery at the level of small networks of cells is mediated by increases in the intrinsic network activity (Barnes et al., 2015) and that intrinsic network activity is amplified within these interconnected neural ensembles (Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The amplification of network activity through a strengthening of network connections may underlie rebalancing of activity in the cortex following sensory deprivation affecting network activity.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the amplification of network activity through a strengthening of network connections may underlie rebalancing of activity in the cortex following sensory deprivation affecting network activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and previous work.

claim: Amplification of network activity provides a mechanism during adulthood by which overall activity can be modulated through the network inputs, without altering the identified sensory inputs and the established circuits thought to drive sensory processing.
source: This provides a mechanism during adulthood by which overall activity can be modulated through the network inputs, without altering the identified sensory inputs and the established circuits thought to drive sensory processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The functional strengthening of network-correlated spines is dependent on the cell-signalling cytokine TNF-α.
source: We find evidence that the functional strengthening of network-correlated spines is dependent on the cell-signalling cytokine TNF-α.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Soluble TNF-α is released from glial cells following reductions in glutamate levels and plays a key role in synaptic strengthening by facilitating the insertion of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPAR).
source: Previous work has shown that soluble TNF-α is released from glial cells following reductions in glutamate levels and plays a key role in synaptic strengthening by facilitating the insertion of α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPAR) (Stellwagen and Malenka, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The synaptic localization of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDAR) and their associated currents are unaffected by changes in TNF-α levels.
source: Importantly, the synaptic localization of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDAR) and their associated currents are unaffected by changes in TNF-α levels (Beattie et al., 2002; He et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of TNF-α has shown selective impairments of homeostatic, but not NMDAR-dependent, Hebbian-like plasticity processes.
source: The specific actions of TNF-α may in part explain in vivo findings, where pharmacological blockade of TNF-α has shown selective impairments of homeostatic, but not NMDAR-dependent, Hebbian-like plasticity processes (Kaneko et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TNF-α-dependent AMPAR insertion during homeostatic regulation is associated with the glutamate receptor-interacting protein 1 (GRIP1).
source: Previous work has shown that TNF-α-dependent AMPAR insertion during homeostatic regulation is associated with the glutamate receptor-interacting protein 1 (GRIP1), a synaptic scaffolding protein which facilitates insertion of synaptic AMPARs, thereby increasing the AMPAR current and number (Barnes et al., 2017; Gainey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AMPAR-mediated synaptic strengthening occurs following monocular enucleation in a TNF-α-dependent manner and involves GRIP1.
source: Increases in GRIP1-dependent AMPAR insertion may be involved in the functional strengthening of spine responses that we observe here, as we have previously demonstrated that AMPAR-mediated synaptic strengthening occurs following monocular enucleation in a TNF-α-dependent manner and involves GRIP1 (Barnes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Inhibitory synapses located on dendritic spines (also containing excitatory synapses) are eliminated at a higher rate following sensory deprivation.
source: Previous work has demonstrated that inhibitory synapses located on dendritic spines (also containing excitatory synapses) are eliminated at a higher rate following sensory deprivation (Chen et al., 2012; van Versendaal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Evidence was found for a reduction in the overall activity of identified sensory responsive spines in visual cortex, with a fraction of visually responsive spines becoming inactive following enucleation.
source: We found evidence for a reduction in the overall activity of identified sensory responsive spines in visual cortex, with a fraction of visually responsive spines becoming inactive following enucleation.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Monocular enucleation is associated with structural spine loss.
source: Our previous work has shown that monocular enucleation is associated with structural spine loss, suggesting that part of the functional silencing we observe here may occur through loss of dendritic spines (Barnes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Part of the functional silencing observed may occur through loss of dendritic spines.
source: Our previous work has shown that monocular enucleation is associated with structural spine loss, suggesting that part of the functional silencing we observe here may occur through loss of dendritic spines (Barnes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from previous work on structural spine loss.

claim: A considerable number of identified sensory responsive spines remain active following sensory deprivation, but undergo no increase in response amplitude, independent of whether they are deprived or non-deprived inputs.
source: A considerable number of identified sensory responsive spines do remain active, but in both visual cortex and RSC, they undergo no increase in response amplitude following sensory deprivation, independent of whether they are deprived or non-deprived inputs.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Identified sensory responsive inputs are not strengthened in sensory cortices following deprivation.
source: Thus, we consistently observe that identified sensory responsive inputs are not strengthened in sensory cortices following deprivation, but that many sensory responsive inputs are preserved, which could underlie the stability of visual tuning that has been observed following sensory deprivation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1; Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Many sensory responsive inputs are preserved following sensory deprivation, which could underlie the stability of visual tuning that has been observed following sensory deprivation.
source: Thus, we consistently observe that identified sensory responsive inputs are not strengthened in sensory cortices following deprivation, but that many sensory responsive inputs are preserved, which could underlie the stability of visual tuning that has been observed following sensory deprivation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1; Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and previous work.

claim: Through homeostatic regulation of the network activity, feedforward sensory input-output relationships that may encode sensory information and underlie sensory processing are not perturbed during adulthood.
source: Through homeostatic regulation of the network activity, feedforward sensory input-output relationships that may encode sensory information and underlie sensory processing are not perturbed during adulthood.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Scaling up the strongest sensory inputs could lead to a saturation of these inputs, due to known dendritic non-linearities in the local integration of multiple inputs.
source: Our previous work (Barnes et al., 2017) has suggested that scaling up the strongest sensory inputs could lead to a saturation of these inputs, due to known dendritic non-linearities in the local integration of multiple inputs (Branco and Häusser, 2011; Branco and Häusser, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: If sensory responsive inputs are saturated and no longer have distinct weights, information processing in the neuron is reduced.
source: If sensory responsive inputs are saturated and no longer have distinct weights, information processing in the neuron is reduced (Barnes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: By homeostatically regulating the network-correlated inputs, the dynamic range of the sensory responsive inputs is unaltered and the cortex can continue to process a wide range of external sensory stimuli.
source: By homeostatically regulating the network-correlated inputs, the dynamic range of the sensory responsive inputs – both the remaining deprived sensory responsive inputs and the non-deprived sensory responsive inputs – is unaltered and the cortex can continue to process a wide range of external sensory stimuli (Panzeri et al., 2017; Panzeri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and previous work.

evidence: This describes the surgical methodology.

source: Mice were injected with AAV2/1-ef1a-GCaMP6s into layer 5 (500 µm deep) before the glass coverslip was positioned.

source: For monocular enucleation, we applied lidocaine (Emla cream) to the area around the left (contralateral) eye in anesthetized mice prior to surgical removal of the eye.

source: For dark exposure experiments, mice were housed in a dark cabinet for 48 hr.

evidence: This describes the experimental timeline.

source: For experiments with the TNF-α inhibitor, mice were injected with XPro1595 (Barnes et al., 2017; Lewitus et al., 2014) (Xencor, Inc) at a dose of 10 mg/kg at –48 and –1 hr for RSC experiments and at −72, –24, and 24 hr for visual cortex experiments.

claim: Functional calcium imaging of volumes of visual cortex or RSC was performed on a custom-built two-photon microscope with a 12 kHz resonance scanner and a high-power objective Z-piezo stage, using a MaiTai eHP laser with a DeepSee prechirp unit set to 910 nm and a Nikon 16×, 0.8 NA objective.
source: Functional calcium imaging of volumes of visual cortex or RSC was performed on a custom-built two-photon microscope with a 12 kHz resonance scanner (Cambridge Technology) and a high-power objective Z-piezo stage (Physik Instrumente), using a MaiTai eHP laser with a DeepSee prechirp unit (Newport/Spectra Physics) set to 910 nm and a Nikon 16×, 0.8 NA objective, as described previously (Barnes et al., 2015).

claim: Mice were presented with drifting gratings in eight directions (0–360 degrees in 45 degree steps) presented in a random order, with a spatial frequency of 0.04 cycles/degree and a temporal frequency of 2 Hz.
source: Mice were presented with drifting gratings in eight directions (0–360 degrees in 45 degree steps) presented in a random order, with a spatial frequency of 0.04 cycles/degree and a temporal frequency of 2 Hz.
evidence: This describes the visual stimulation methodology.

claim: Auditory stimulation consisted of the presentation of bilateral white noise bursts at 65 dB presented 30 cm from the mouse's ears, with timing according to a uniform distribution (minimum interval of 3 s and maximum interval of 5 s).
source: Auditory stimulation consisted of the presentation of bilateral white noise bursts at 65 dB presented 30 cm from the mouse's ears, with timing according to a uniform distribution (minimum interval of 3 s and maximum interval of 5 s).
evidence: This describes the auditory stimulation methodology.

claim: Calcium responses from individual spines were isolated from global dendritic signals using a subtraction procedure described previously.
source: Calcium responses from individual spines were isolated from global dendritic signals using a subtraction procedure described previously (Chen et al., 2013b; Iacaruso et al., 2017; Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology.

claim: Spines were determined to be visually responsive if they responded to either set of visual stimuli (gratings or sparse noise).
source: To define functional properties of spines in visual cortex, we first classified spines as visual or not based on their responses to visual gratings and a sparse noise stimulus. Spines were determined to be visually responsive if they responded to either set of visual stimuli.
evidence: This describes the classification methodology.

claim: The correlation of the spine calcium fluorescence signal with a binarized visual stimulation signal was computed to determine visual responsiveness.
source: We next determined if spines were responsive to the visual gratings (Barnes et al., 2015; Ko et al., 2011). We first computed the correlation of the spine calcium fluorescence signal with a binarized visual stimulation signal that corresponds to the timing of the stimulus.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology.

claim: The correlation coefficient between individual spine ΔF/F0 signals and a network average ΔF/F0 signal was calculated to classify network-correlated spines.
source: To classify network-correlated spines, we calculated the correlation coefficient between individual spine ΔF/F0 signals and a network average ΔF/F0 signal comprising of the average of all spine signals during all conditions in the imaged cortical region, excluding the spine of interest (based on Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology.

claim: Spine ΔF/F0 signals were determined to be correlated with the network signal if the correlation value was positive and significant (p<0.05).
source: Spine ΔF/F0 signals were determined to be correlated with the network signal if the correlation value was positive and significant (p<0.05).
evidence: This describes the statistical criteria for classification.

claim: 99% of the spines that were identified as network-correlated, but not visually responsive, had fewer stimulus-locked visual responses than the false positive threshold.
source: Using the same visual stimulation threshold criteria mentioned above, 99% of the spines that were identified as network-correlated, but not visually responsive, had fewer stimulus-locked visual responses than our false positive threshold, and non-significant visual correlations.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis validating the classification method.

claim: Few unclassified spines had significant correlations with either whisker movement (3.2%) or pupil position or diameter (1.4%).
source: Unclassified spines in both brain regions had no significant correlation with the external stimuli or network signal. Few unclassified spines had significant correlations with either whisker movement (3.2%) or pupil position or diameter (1.4%).
